x: Notes

Branchy leaves are guaranteed to drop a stick. They also have a higher chance to drop seeds. The chance is unaffected by tool used to harvest them. Unlike normal leaf blocks, branchy leaves willcount against axe durability when cutting down a tree, if still connected to the trunk.
Notes

leaf blocks have a smaller chance to drop sticks and seeds than branchy leaf blocks. The chance is unaffected by tool used to harvest them. Unlike branchy leaf blocks, regular leaves will notcount against axe durability when cutting down a tree.
How to Use

- Place the raft with a Right mouse click.
- Right mouse click on the raft to board it.
- With an oar in your active hotbar slot, you can move the raft.
- Disembark from the raft using the Shift key.
- Pick up the raft using the Shift button combined with a Right mouse click.
How to Construct

Sailboats are constructed in place on land, and then rolled into the water. They cannot be picked up. They can be deconstructed by holding down Right mouse with a saw. See the Building A Sailboat entry for more information.

Movement
Once you have constructed your sailboat, Right mouse click on the starboard aft seat (by the tiller at the stern) to sit in that seat: only that seat can control the boat. With the sails furled, you can use normal navigation keys to move the boat slowly. Right mouse-click on the cleat on the side of the mast (where a rope is tied) to unfurl the sail and pick up speed. The sailboat currently does not respond to wind direction, only your movement keys.

If the boat becomes grounded or in water that is too shallow, it can be moved very slowly using the arrow keys, but only with the sail furled again.

Equipping
Most boat accessories are added to the boat via Ctrl + Right mouse.
The boat can also hold several passengers - in every boat, one passenger can sit on the port-side aft seat (adjacent to the player who is at the tiller controlling the boat). Additional seats can be added to any of the eight cargo hold spots.

You can place containers (including chests, baskets, and storage vessels) in the hold of the boat, and access them on or off the boat.

You can also place a mount (such as an elk) on the boat by first placing a wooden fence post in one of the cargo spots - being sure to leave 2 cargo spots empty aft of the post - and then using a rope on this fence post, which will place the animal into the aft cargo spots. You can then disembark the animal using Right mouse on the fence post.

You can attach a lantern to the aft face of the mast (about 3 meters up) to provide light.

Ratlines can be attached to the gunwhales on each side of the mast in order to allow you to climb to the top of the mast to look around.

An anchor can be placed in the front-left space in the prow (though currently the anchor has no function).

There is also a spot at the prow for a figurehead to be placed (you can also place your own chiseled figurehead there), and on the port bow, your boat can be named (using pigment and Shift + Right mouse-click).
Notes

Tree seed drop chance is unaffected by tool used to harvest the leaf block, however, if you fell an entire tree with an axe you will get far fewer seeds than if you had broken the leaf blocks first. Branchy leaves have a higher chance to drop seeds, compared to normal leaf blocks.

x: Alcohol Aging Guide (Expanded Foods)

All alcohols now cure over time. If it finishes curing before it begins to perish into vinegar, then it progresses to the next stage, becoming more intoxicating and filling.
Ciders and ales (usually created from curing juice or sealing it in a barrel) cure into 'strong' alcohol, then into 'fine' alcohol.
Spirits, such as brandy and whiskey (created by distilling cider/ale in a boiler), cure into 'aged' alcohol, then into 'vintage' alcohol.
'Fine' alcohol can still spoil if improperly stored - make sure it's stored someplace cool so it can 'cure' into itself instead of spoiling into vinegar. 'Vintage' alcohol lasts indefinitely, due to the concentrated alcohol content.
Care and Propagation of Fruiting Bushes

Propagation:
Wild fruiting bushes cannot be moved - if you break them they will just drop plant debris. However you can propagate them by obtaining a cutting (via Shift + Right mouse-clicking with a knife) and planting that cutting in regular soil (not farmland). The fertility of the soil they are planted on will affect the initial health of the bush when the cutting matures.
You can only take one cutting per bush, per year. The cuttings will take 4-8 months to grow into a fully mature bush capable of fruiting.
Some invidiviual bushes can have special traits that make them better or worse in some aspects than others, and these characteristics will be propagated along with the cutting. Note that cuttings with different traits will not stack in inventory.
Care:
Fruit bushes can have four health states: bountiful, healthy, struggling, and barren. The more healthy the bush, the more fruit it will yield, and the health status will be reflected in the quantity of flowers and fruit visible on the bush.
Wild bushes will only be found in the healthy or struggling states. The health of wild bushes cannot be changed, and you cannot add fertilizer to them. Propagated bushes however, can have their health improved by fertilization (or conversely, worsened by neglect). Unlike crops, fertilizer is applied directly to the bush, and not the soil underneath. Fruiting bushes will also use any fertilizer, they are not limited to just one as crops are. Fruiting bushes do not require watering, unlike crops, nor do the nutrients of the bushes replenish yearly the way farmland does.
Each time a propagated bush produces a harvest, it will use up some of the fertilizer that has been applied to it. If the total fertilizer (the sum of all 3 nutrients applied to the bush) falls below certain threshholds, the bush will decline in health. The levels of fertilization are as follows:

above 80%: bountiful (150% yield)
30-80%: healthy (100% yield)
10-30%: struggling (50% yield)
Below 10%: barren (no yield)

The health will not necessarily decline every harvest, and a bush would in most cases require several years of continual harvest and no fertilization to go from bountiful to barren health. In the long term, a propagated bush's need for fertilizer will decline over time, until after about 20 years they will need hardly any.
Juice Processing Guide (Expanded Foods)

Fruit juice is a base liquid with many resulting outputs.
If allowed to spoil, it ferments into vinegar and acidifies.
When sealed into a barrel or bottle, juice cures over time into 'cider' (the exact name varies based on the fruit used).
Lastly, juice may be simmered in a saucepan or cauldron to concentrate it into fruit syrup.
Alcohol Aging Guide (Expanded Foods)

All alcohols now cure over time. If it finishes curing before it begins to perish into vinegar, then it progresses to the next stage, becoming more intoxicating and filling.
Ciders and ales (usually created from curing juice or sealing it in a barrel) cure into 'strong' alcohol, then into 'fine' alcohol.
Spirits, such as brandy and whiskey (created by distilling cider/ale in a boiler), cure into 'aged' alcohol, then into 'vintage' alcohol.
'Fine' alcohol can still spoil if improperly stored - make sure it's stored someplace cool so it can 'cure' into itself instead of spoiling into vinegar. 'Vintage' alcohol lasts indefinitely, due to the concentrated alcohol content.

x: Uses

Cassava is a useful vegetable, it can be added as a starchy vegetable to meals, or dried and ground to make flour. The Cassava plant tolerates most warm climates and yields a good quantity of the crop.

Raw cassava is toxic, however. To make it safe to eat, it must first be soaked in water for a day (hint: use a barrel). The Soaked cassava must be peeled with a knife. Cassava can then be added to meals as a vegetable. Once peeled, it must be used within a few hours or else it will start to dry out. When dried its only use is to be ground to make Cassava flour.

x: Crafting

Bricks can be fired in a pit kiln, which will give a limited set of colors. They can also be fired in a beehive kiln, which will allow a much greater range of colors to be made. Furthermore, the larger format bricks of 4 courses per block, can be crafted to a smaller size that has double the courses.

Polychromy

different colors of bricks can be combined via chiseling, and 3 basic patterns can be made - running, soldier, and header bonds. Each of these bonds can also be switched to an offset variant, and running bonds have an additional two variants (1/4 offset and 3/4 offset). Via the use of these three basic patterns and their offsets, virtually any pattern of brickwork can be made. Research 'brick polychromy' to learn more.

Fruit bushes can have four health states: bountiful, healthy, struggling, and barren. The more healthy the bush, the more fruit it will yield, and the health status will be reflected in the quantity of flowers and fruit visible on the bush.
Wild bushes will only be found in the healthy or struggling states. The health of wild bushes cannot be changed, and you cannot add fertilizer to them. Propagated bushes however, can have their health improved by fertilization (or conversely, worsened by neglect). Unlike crops, fertilizer is applied directly to the bush, and not the soil underneath. Fruiting bushes will also use any fertilizer, they are not limited to just one as crops are. Fruiting bushes do not require watering, unlike crops, nor do the nutrients of the bushes replenish yearly the way farmland does.
Each time a propagated bush produces a harvest, it will use up some of the fertilizer that has been applied to it. If the total fertilizer (the sum of all 3 nutrients applied to the bush) falls below certain threshholds, the bush will decline in health. The levels of fertilization are as follows:

above 80%: bountiful (150% yield)
30-80%: healthy (100% yield)
10-30%: struggling (50% yield)
Below 10%: barren (no yield)

The health will not necessarily decline every harvest, and a bush would in most cases require several years of continual harvest and no fertilization to go from bountiful to barren health. In the long term, a propagated bush's need for fertilizer will decline over time, until after about 20 years they will need hardly any.
Juice Processing Guide (Expanded Foods)

Fruit juice is a base liquid with many resulting outputs.
If allowed to spoil, it ferments into vinegar and acidifies.
When sealed into a barrel or bottle, juice cures over time into 'cider' (the exact name varies based on the fruit used).
Lastly, juice may be simmered in a saucepan or cauldron to concentrate it into fruit syrup.
Alcohol Aging Guide (Expanded Foods)

All alcohols now cure over time. If it finishes curing before it begins to perish into vinegar, then it progresses to the next stage, becoming more intoxicating and filling.
Ciders and ales (usually created from curing juice or sealing it in a barrel) cure into 'strong' alcohol, then into 'fine' alcohol.
Spirits, such as brandy and whiskey (created by distilling cider/ale in a boiler), cure into 'aged' alcohol, then into 'vintage' alcohol.
'Fine' alcohol can still spoil if improperly stored - make sure it's stored someplace cool so it can 'cure' into itself instead of spoiling into vinegar. 'Vintage' alcohol lasts indefinitely, due to the concentrated alcohol content.

How to Construct

Sailboats are constructed in place on land, and then rolled into the water. They cannot be picked up. They can be deconstructed by holding down Right mouse with a saw. See the Building A Sailboat entry for more information.

Movement
Once you have constructed your sailboat, Right mouse click on the starboard aft seat (by the tiller at the stern) to sit in that seat: only that seat can control the boat. With the sails furled, you can use normal navigation keys to move the boat slowly. Right mouse-click on the cleat on the side of the mast (where a rope is tied) to unfurl the sail and pick up speed. The sailboat currently does not respond to wind direction, only your movement keys.

If the boat becomes grounded or in water that is too shallow, it can be moved very slowly using the arrow keys, but only with the sail furled again.

Equipping
Most boat accessories are added to the boat via Ctrl + Right mouse.
The boat can also hold several passengers - in every boat, one passenger can sit on the port-side aft seat (adjacent to the player who is at the tiller controlling the boat). Additional seats can be added to any of the eight cargo hold spots.

You can place containers (including chests, baskets, and storage vessels) in the hold of the boat, and access them on or off the boat.

You can also place a mount (such as an elk) on the boat by first placing a wooden fence post in one of the cargo spots - being sure to leave 2 cargo spots empty aft of the post - and then using a rope on this fence post, which will place the animal into the aft cargo spots. You can then disembark the animal using Right mouse on the fence post.

You can attach a lantern to the aft face of the mast (about 3 meters up) to provide light.

Ratlines can be attached to the gunwhales on each side of the mast in order to allow you to climb to the top of the mast to look around.

An anchor can be placed in the front-left space in the prow (though currently the anchor has no function).

There is also a spot at the prow for a figurehead to be placed (you can also place your own chiseled figurehead there), and on the port bow, your boat can be named (using pigment and Shift + Right mouse-click).
Notes

Tree seed drop chance is unaffected by tool used to harvest the leaf block, however, if you fell an entire tree with an axe you will get far fewer seeds than if you had broken the leaf blocks first. Branchy leaves have a higher chance to drop seeds, compared to normal leaf blocks.
How to Use

Basket traps will catch many (but not all) baby animals, and smaller adult animals such as chickens and hares. The trap must be baited with a food item appropriate to the target animal. The traps do not always work, sometimes the animals will trigger them but not be caught. Some adult animals can take the food without being caught, or even trample the traps. Once an animal is successfully caught in the trap, you can carry it in the basket. To pick up and carry the basket, Right mouse-click it: you will need one of your four backpack slots free for this. To release the carried animal, select the basket (use hotkey Ctrl + 1, 2, 3, or 4 depending on which backpack slot it is in). Right mouse-click on the spot where you want it released.

Be aware that an animal, once trapped, will die after some time, normally 24 hours - if it dies you will get its corpse though. If you release and re-trap the animal, the death timer only resets if the animal was released and free for at least the same amount of time that it was already in the trap.

A wood crate trap will catch larger animals than a basket trap, but is still too small to catch many adult animals. The bait is held high at the back of the cavity, so many smaller animals that will enter a basket trap, will not be attracted to this trap, since they cannot reach the bait. Since the rope is tied to the bait, tiny baits like grains cannot be used with the crate trap.

To release the carried animal, select the crate (use hotkey Ctrl + 1, 2, 3, or 4 depending on which backpack slot it is in). Right mouse-click on the spot where you want it released.

Be aware that an animal, once trapped, will die if left in the trap for too long; normally 24 hours - if it dies you will get its corpse though. Where to find

Resin is found leaking from the trunks of pine and acacia trees. Pines can be found in all but the most inhospitable and extreme climates, while acacias are found in dry tropical climates only. Resin is also an ingredient for pitch glue.

Liquid resin can be collected from acacia/pine trees using a spile.
Pine trees produce resin from March to November.
Acacia trees produce resin from April to September.
